title: Air India Just Posted a ₹26,000 Crore Loss — and the Tata Turnaround Story Has Never Looked More Fragile
excerpt: Fuel spikes, airspace closures, and a fleet still mid-overhaul have turned the national carrier's recovery plan into a survival exercise. For NRIs who depend on its routes, the consequences are already being felt.
body:
Air India's financial results for FY2025-26, disclosed quietly this month, reveal a loss exceeding ₹26,000 crore ($3 billion) — making it one of the worst annual performances by any airline in the Asia-Pacific region this fiscal year. The number is staggering even by the standards of a carrier that has spent most of its existence in the red.

The immediate causes are well known: the Iran-US conflict has closed West Asian airspace since early 2026, forcing Air India to reroute dozens of flights on its most profitable corridors. Jet fuel prices have surged past $130 per barrel for the first time since 2014. And the Pakistani airspace restrictions, intermittently reimposed since the Pahalgam tensions, have added further costs on routes to Europe and Central Asia.

But the deeper story is structural. When Tata Sons acquired Air India in January 2022 for ₹18,000 crore, the promise was a five-year transformation — new aircraft, better service, rationalized routes, and a path to profitability by 2027. That timeline now looks impossibly optimistic.

## The Fleet Trap

Air India's fleet modernization was supposed to be its competitive weapon. The airline ordered 470 new aircraft from Airbus and Boeing in February 2023 — the largest order in aviation history. But deliveries have been painfully slow. Boeing's production crises and Airbus's engine supply constraints mean that Air India is still operating a significant proportion of its fleet with ageing, fuel-inefficient aircraft that were inherited from the government era.

Meanwhile, maintenance costs have ballooned. Several wide-body aircraft have been grounded for extended periods awaiting parts. The Vistara merger, completed in late 2024, added complexity — different crew training standards, incompatible IT systems, and a culture clash between Vistara's premium-focused staff and Air India's legacy workforce.

## The Route Surgery

CEO Campbell Wilson has responded with aggressive cost-cutting. Air India has announced service reductions across international routes from June to August 2026, including reduced frequencies to Chicago, San Francisco, and several European destinations. Salary hikes have been deferred by a quarter. Non-technical staff face pay freezes.

For the 4.4 million-strong Indian American community, the route cuts are personal. Air India remains the only non-stop option on several India-US city pairs, particularly from smaller Indian cities. Reduced frequencies mean higher fares during peak travel seasons — the summer months when NRI families traditionally visit India.

## Singapore Airlines's Awkward Position

Singapore Airlines, which holds a 25.1% stake in Air India following the Vistara merger, is watching from the sidelines with increasing discomfort. SIA's own results have been solid — revenue of S$16 billion and a healthy net margin — but the Air India investment is effectively underwater. The carrier has so far declined to inject additional capital, and industry analysts say the relationship is being "managed, not nurtured."

The Tata Group, for its part, has signalled willingness to absorb losses in the near term. Group chairman N. Chandrasekaran has repeatedly described Air India as a "generational project." But at ₹26,000 crore in annual losses, even Tata's deep pockets face limits.

**What to watch:** Air India's survival through the current crisis depends on two factors outside its control: the Iran conflict (which determines fuel prices and airspace access) and Boeing's delivery schedule. If either improves in H2 2026, the airline's trajectory could shift dramatically. If neither does, expect deeper cuts — and louder questions about the Tata acquisition's wisdom.
